issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should give due weight to a trial court’s findings on disputed oral evidence when the trial court observed the witnesses, unless a material error or other sufficient reason justifies interference.
material_facts: The adoption dispute turned principally on conflicting oral testimony.
The trial court analysed the material witnesses and assessed their testimony in light of the surrounding circumstances and the witnesses’ demeanour.
The High Court reversed the trial court’s factual finding without adequate grounds, and its assessment overlooked material evidence and proceeded on a misdirection about the standard of proof.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had no adequate ground to displace the trial court’s finding that the adoption had been proved; that finding was restored.
issues.legal_principle: A trial judge’s opportunity to observe witnesses is a cogent circumstance when credibility is in issue, and the trial court’s finding should ordinarily prevail in such a case unless a special feature was overlooked or there is a sufficient balance of improbability. An appellate court may nevertheless interfere where the trial court’s appraisal has a material irregularity, rests on inadmissible evidence or a misreading of evidence, or relies on conjecture or surmise. The Court relied on W.C. Macdonald v. Fred Latimer, Watt v. Thomas, Sara Veeraswami v. Talluri Narayya, Sarju Parshad v. Raja Jwaleshwari Pratap Narain Singh, and The Asiatic Steam Navigation Co. Ltd. v. Sub-Lt. Arabindra Chakravarti.

rule.if: civil_appeal_from_trial_court_finding and disputed_oral_evidence_turns_on_credibility and trial_court_observed_witnesses and not material_error_in_trial_appraisal

predicates.civil_appeal_from_trial_court_finding: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a trial court’s factual finding.
predicates.disputed_oral_evidence_turns_on_credibil: The disputed issue depends on conflicting oral testimony and the credibility of witnesses.
predicates.trial_court_observed_witnesses: The trial court saw and heard the witnesses while they testified.
predicates.material_error_in_trial_appraisal: The trial court’s appraisal contains a material irregularity, relies on inadmissible evidence or a misreading of evidence, or rests on conjecture or surmise.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a trial finding based on credibility in oral evidence, the finding should ordinarily prevail if the trial court observed the witnesses and its appraisal contains no material error.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to the party who called the witness, or possible prejudice against the opposing party, does not by itself justify rejecting the witness’s evidence.
material_facts: The High Court substantially rejected witnesses supporting the adoption because they were related to the appellant or were said to be out of favour with the opposing side.
The trial court had assessed their testimony in the context of the evidence as a whole and had the opportunity to observe their demeanour.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s relationship-based approach to credibility was erroneous; the evidence had to be assessed cautiously against the entire record rather than rejected on relationship or possible prejudice alone.
issues.legal_principle: A court must exercise appropriate caution when assessing a witness who is related to the party calling the witness or may be prejudiced against the opposing party, and must evaluate the evidence against the entire mosaic of facts. It is not open to reject the evidence on relationship, favour, or possible prejudice alone. The Court also said due consideration was owed to the trial court’s opportunity to observe the witnesses.

predicates.witness_credibility_assessment: The court is assessing the credibility and probative value of a witness’s testimony.
predicates.witness_related_to_calling_party_or_poss: The witness is related to the party calling the witness or may be prejudiced against the opposing party.
predicates.no_independent_reason_for_rejection: There is no reason for rejecting the testimony beyond the witness’s relationship, favour, or possible prejudice.

issues.definition: In a credibility assessment, a related or possibly prejudiced witness’s testimony is not rejected solely on that basis when there is no independent reason for rejection.

issues.legal_issue: An adoption is proved and valid when the required transfer and acceptance of the child are established by reliable evidence and the applicable custom does not require an additional ceremony.
material_facts: The appellant claimed to have been adopted by a childless couple, and the central factual dispute was whether the adoption ceremony had occurred.

The trial court accepted evidence that the natural parent gave the appellant and the adoptive parents received him, and relied on oral and documentary evidence, including a deed signed by both adoptive parents on the day of the alleged adoption and a later letter in which the adoptive father accepted the appellant as his son.

The trial court found that the appellant’s community custom required the ceremony of giving and taking but not the datta homam ceremony; the Supreme Court found nothing showing that an additional ceremony was necessary.
The adoptive mother was seriously ill, and the circumstances did not permit elaborate arrangements, invitations, or ceremonies.
issues.conclusion: The adoption was proved in fact and was valid in law; the trial court’s finding was restored.
issues.legal_principle: A person alleging adoption bears the burden of proving both the factum and validity of the adoption. The evidence must be free from suspicion of fraud and sufficiently consistent and probable, but adoption is proved in the same way as any other fact. Under Hindu law, actual giving and taking is an essential requisite in every adoption; consent or an executed deed alone does not suffice. No particular form is prescribed, and the ceremony may vary with the circumstances. A further datta homam ceremony is required only where applicable law or custom requires it. The Court relied on A. Raghavamma v. A. Chenchamma, Kishori Lal v. Chaltibai, Shoshinath v. Krishnasunder, Lakshman Singh v. Smt. Rupkanwar, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak v. Shriniwas Pandit.

rule.if: adoption_claim_in_property_dispute and actual_giving_and_taking_proved and adoption_evidence_consistent_and_probable and applicable_custom_requires_no_additional_ceremony

predicates.adoption_claim_in_property_dispute: A party claims adoption as the basis for a right in a property dispute.
predicates.actual_giving_and_taking_proved: Evidence establishes that the natural parent transferred the child and the adoptive parent received the child.
predicates.adoption_evidence_consistent_and_probabl: The evidence of adoption is consistent and probable and does not give reason to suspect fraud.
predicates.applicable_custom_requires_no_additional: The applicable custom does not require a ceremony beyond giving and taking.

issues.definition: An adoption claimed in a property dispute is proved and valid when actual giving and taking is established by consistent and probable evidence and the applicable custom requires no additional ceremony.

issues.legal_issue: A separation from a joint Hindu family by unilateral intention requires a clear and unequivocal communication of that intention to the affected co-sharers.
material_facts: A trust deed contained a declaration of an intention to separate if the alleged adoption were later declared valid.
There was no evidence that the intention to separate was communicated to the appellant when the trust was created.
issues.conclusion: The declaration in the trust deed did not effect a separation because the intention to separate was not communicated to the co-sharer.
issues.legal_principle: A separation is effected by a clear and unequivocal intimation of the member’s desire to sever to the co-sharers; the intention must be manifested to the knowledge of the persons affected, since an uncommunicated intention has no effect. The Court relied on Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, Bal Krishan v. Ram Krishan, A. Raghavamma v. Chenchamma, Puttrangamma v. M.S. Ranganna, and Kalyani v. Narayanan.

predicates.joint_family_separation_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim that a member separated from a joint Hindu family.
predicates.unilateral_intention_to_separate: A member expressed a clear and unequivocal intention to separate from the family.
predicates.intention_communicated_to_affected_co_sh: The member communicated the intention to separate to the co-sharer affected by it.

issues.definition: A unilateral intention to separate does not effect separation when it is not communicated to the affected co-sharer.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise made before an heir’s claimed share vests does not establish that the heir relinquished that later-vesting right.
material_facts: A compromise had been reached in litigation concerning the trust before the death on which the claimed one-fourth share depended.
The claimed right vested only on that death.
issues.conclusion: The compromise did not bar the heir’s claim to the share, because the right had not vested when the compromise was made.
issues.legal_principle: The Court agreed with the High Court that a person could not be regarded as having given up a right that vested only after the compromise. No earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this point.

predicates.claim_by_heir_under_prior_compromise: An heir’s claim is said to be barred by a compromise made in earlier litigation.
predicates.claimed_right_vested_after_compromise: The right claimed by the heir vested only after the compromise was made.

issues.definition: A prior compromise does not relinquish an heir’s claimed right when that right vested only after the compromise.

issues.legal_issue: The partition suit was not barred by limitation.
material_facts: The trial court held that the suit was not barred by limitation.
The High Court agreed with that conclusion, and no serious argument on limitation was raised in the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court affirmed the conclusion that the suit was not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court agreed with the lower courts’ limitation determination but stated no further limitation analysis, statutory provision, or earlier case on that issue.

predicates.partition_suit_on_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a suit seeking partition and separate possession.
predicates.trial_court_found_suit_not_time_barred: The trial court found that the suit was not barred by limitation.
predicates.appellate_court_agreed: The appellate court agreed with the trial court’s conclusion on limitation.

issues.definition: A partition suit is treated as not barred by limitation when the trial court so found and the appellate court agreed.
